prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks and their development to the 10^-18 level of precision, opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: Four of us put B001 first, and I do so again after reading the other seven ballots. The discovery is that atoms held in a magic-wavelength lattice can be interrogated by many thousands at once with light shifts cancelled, which brought fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. That is a result nature itself checks: clocks in different laboratories agree, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift is resolved, and clocks now set limits on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings. It is exactly the kind of clue from nature that I want a prize to rest on. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. Katori proposed and first realised the scheme; Ye's group carried it to record accuracy and stability. All seven members who ranked B001 proposed the same two names, and nobody argues that a third person is needed. Maturity is good: many independent labs, years of cross-comparisons, and a stable interpretation.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, raised in my own opening and by Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce, is that this may read as a refinement of areas already honoured (frequency combs in 2005, ion clocks in 2012) rather than a new discovery. A second reservation is that other groups (SYRTE, NIST, PTB, the Ludlow, Bloom and Hinkley line of work) were decisive for specific milestones and a two-name prize leaves them out. Finally, the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue for waiting. I think none of these overturn the case, but the first needs a citation that stresses the lattice-clock concept and its consequences rather than clock accuracy alone.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B001 first but would like the redefinition of the SI second to be well advanced, and also puts the Higgs detector conception (B002) second, with attribution fairness as the main issue.
responses.response: I share the wish to see the second redefinition proceed, but I do not think the prize should wait for it. The physics is established and the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows from the discovery, not a condition for it. On B002 I respect the achievement, but I remain uneasy: the discovery was made by thousands, the 2013 prize already recognised the mechanism, and honouring conception and construction by three founders-leaders will be hard to defend as the discoverers. I would keep it as a later option, not first in line.

responses.point: Mehlig puts the defect-mediated 2D melting theory (B006) first as a simple, general mechanism extending the 2016 line, while ranking B001 second.
responses.response: I appreciate the elegance of Halperin-Nelson-Young, and the idea is surely foundational. But my reservations are the ones Mehlig himself lists: the hexatic scenario is qualified by first-order melting in several systems, it sits very close to the 2016 prize, and the three-name credit is difficult given Kosterlitz and Thouless. With only one first-place vote and no other member ranking it, I cannot see it being the stronger basis for a prize this year than something confirmed so cleanly by measurement.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B001 first for atomic-precision reasons but worries that the combs (2005) and ion clocks (2012) make the area feel already honoured, and puts B042 second.
responses.response: I take the overlap worry seriously, but think it is answered by what is new: Hall and Hansch gave us the comb that counts optical cycles, Wineland the single-ion clock, while the lattice clock opened a genuinely different regime of many-atom interrogation, with systematic control that makes relativistic geodesy and constant searches feasible. As for B042, I agree on the conceptual elegance, yet my own ranking put it sixth: choosing three of five is arbitrary, and the payoff, solving problems beyond classical computation, has not yet been shown.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B003) first and B001 fifth, stressing that cQED is the architecture of superconducting processors, while acknowledging proximity to the 2025 prize and flagging his own ties to this community.
responses.response: I agree cQED is a clean and reproduced piece of physics, and Johansson deserves credit for flagging his connection frankly. My difficulty is not quality but timing and allocation: the 2025 prize on circuits is fresh, the four-person credit forces the exclusion of Girvin or a theorist, and I gave it only eighth place. I would be less worried about B001 being 'merely technological' than about B003 being close to what we have just honoured. Where we may agree is that B001 is a measurement of nature, while B003 is mostly an engineering architecture.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B010) first and magic-angle graphene (B017) second, emphasising Kane-Mele with the HgTe confirmation as a new class of matter.
responses.response: The Kane-Mele-Molenkamp story is a very strong one, and the quantitative HgTe confirmation is what I like. But Eriksson's own uncertainty is exactly my worry: credit is split among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan, and three names cannot represent that, and three overlapping topological candidates (B010, B004) remain on the table. I put B017 fourth for reasons close to his, but I find the unresolved pairing mechanism a reason to wait, whereas B001 offers fewer open issues.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see lattice clocks as a distinct discovery rather than an extension of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.
Whether other clock groups have a claim so decisive that a Katori-Ye prize is unfair to them.
For the fallback B045, whether the BeppoSAX X-ray and Kulkarni optical credit is adequately captured without van Paradijs and Piro.
As Secretary I would still want external expert reports to confirm the priority record of the magic-wavelength proposal.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B045 or B017. My Uppsala string-theory background, supervisor David Gross and collaborator Thomas Van Riet have no link to any candidate named on the shortlist.
